teaser: She has already walked past. Then she glances over her shoulder, and three centuries stop.
review_notes:
Dimensions 63 x 31.2 cm, color on silk, hanging scroll (Tokyo National Museum).
Date: usually given as late 17th century (Genroku era), c. 1688-1694; catalog says 1690.
Hairstyle (tamamusubi) and obi knot (Kichiya-musubi, after the actor Uemura Kichiya) per museum descriptions.
Signature read as 'Boyo Hishikawa Tomotake'; Boyo refers to his native Awa/Boshu province (Hota, Chiba).
1948 stamp: issued for Philatelic Week, much sought after by collectors.
Moronobu illustrated well over 100 books: figure varies by source.

lesson.text: What makes you turn around in the street? A voice you know, a sound, the feeling of being watched? This young woman was walking away when something caught her. The painter gives no hint of what it was. He only kept the turn.
And he kept very little else. No ground under her feet, no wall, no tree, no shadow. Hishikawa Moronobu set one figure on bare silk and trusted her outline to do everything. So follow the outline.
A body that goes one way and a glance that goes the other.

lines.label: Her path
lines.text: The big knot of her sash is on her back, and her back is toward us. She is heading away, to the left. Her long sleeve swings out in that direction.

lines.label: Her glance
lines.text: Her head swivels the opposite way, over her right shoulder. Whatever caught her attention is somewhere off the edge of the silk.

lines.label: The curve
lines.text: Head, shoulders, hips and trailing hem bend into a long S. That twist is the whole action of the picture: a step paused halfway.

lines.label: Nothing
lines.text: Almost a third of the scroll above her is empty. The space gives her room to move and makes her seem smaller, lighter, caught in passing.

lesson.text: Showing her from behind was a practical choice as much as a poetic one. From the back, a kimono displays everything a fashionable person in Edo wanted to check: the pattern across the shoulders, the way the sash was tied, the hair. In a way the scroll is a fashion plate, and every item on it was the latest thing around 1690.
Moronobu grew up among luxury fabrics. His father embroidered and gilded rich textiles in a fishing village on Tokyo Bay, and the son trained in the family trade before he ever became a painter.

lesson.title: Dressed for 1690
lesson.text: Three things a viewer of the time would have noticed immediately, and one written in the margin.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: Worn long down the back and tied at the end into a glossy loop, with a comb and a white ribbon on top. This looped style was popular with young townswomen.

spots.title: The sash
spots.text: A green sash with a flower pattern, tied so its ends droop like a dog's ears. The knot was named after a kabuki actor who played women's roles and set trends by doing so.

spots.title: The kimono
spots.text: Scarlet, scattered with round chrysanthemums and cherry blossoms in white, blue and gold. The long hanging sleeves mark a young, unmarried woman.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: Down the right side, the painter signs with his name and adds his home province. He was proud of where he came from.

lesson.text: None of this is a print. Moronobu is often called the founder of ukiyo-e, the “pictures of the floating world” that celebrated the pleasures of city life. He was one of the first to sell single printed sheets and he illustrated well over a hundred books. But this is a one-off painting in ink and color on silk, about 63 centimeters tall (25 inches), made for a client with money.
Ukiyo-e began with a shift of subject. Instead of sages, saints or landscapes, a painter looked at an ordinary, anonymous young woman in the street and decided she was enough.

Why paint her at all? Edo was then barely a century old as a capital and already one of the largest cities on earth. Its merchants were officially the lowest social class, yet they had the cash. They spent it on theater, clothes and pictures of people like themselves.

She has no name, and that is part of the novelty. She is not a goddess, a court lady from an old poem, or a famous courtesan. She is a type: a well-dressed girl of the merchant class in the biggest city in Japan, enjoying being looked at.

In 1948 Japan put her on a postage stamp, unusually large for the time. It became one of the most sought-after stamps among Japanese collectors, and it made this scroll familiar to people who had never entered a museum.

Every later beauty in Japanese art, from Utamaro's close-ups to modern advertising, descends in some way from this small scroll. And the question it opened with still has no answer. What did she hear?

quiz.question: What is this work made of?
options: Ink and color painted on silk
quiz.explanation: It is a unique painting on a silk hanging scroll, not a print.

quiz.question: How do we know she is walking away from us?
options: The knot of her sash, worn on the back, faces us
She casts a shadow behind her
quiz.explanation: We see her back, and her head turns over her shoulder.

quiz.question: What does ukiyo-e mean?
quiz.explanation: It celebrated the pleasures and fashions of city life.

quiz.question: What do the long hanging sleeves indicate?
quiz.explanation: Long sleeves were worn by young unmarried women.

quiz.question: What did Moronobu's father do?
quiz.explanation: Moronobu trained in the family textile trade first.

facts.text: The background shows a street in Edo.
facts.explanation: There is no setting at all, only bare silk.

facts.text: The woman in the painting is a named historical celebrity.
facts.explanation: She is anonymous, a fashionable type from the merchant class.

facts.text: The painting was reproduced on a Japanese postage stamp in 1948.
facts.explanation: The stamp made the image famous well beyond museums.
